lessons.title: The whip-and-tongue graft: step-by-step with local fruit trees
lessons.body:
The whip-and-tongue graft is the best choice for beginners because it gives strong, natural-looking unions on young, flexible wood. Use it when your scion (the variety you want) and rootstock (the base tree) are both pencil-thick (about 6â10 mm diameter) and dormant. In Africa, this works well for mango, avocado, citrus, and guava. Start in early spring before buds break, or during the cool dry season if you can irrigate.

First, collect scion wood from a healthy, productive tree of the variety you want. Choose last season's growth that is firm and green-brown, not soft. Cut 20â30 cm lengths with at least 3 buds. Keep them wrapped in damp cloth in a cooler until you graft. For rootstock, use a seedling of the same species that is at least 30 cm tall and 6â10 mm thick at the point where you will graft.

Make the cuts: Hold the rootstock firmly. With a sharp, clean grafting knife, make a smooth, 4â5 cm long diagonal cut on one side of the rootstock, starting about 2 cm below the top. The cut should be flat and straight. Then make a similar cut on the scion, but slightly shorter (3â4 cm). Now the 'tongue': on the rootstock cut, start about one-third from the top and slice down into the wood, making a 1â2 cm deep slit. Do the same on the scion, but slice upward. The tongues should interlock.

Slide the two pieces together so the tongues lock and the cambium layers (the green layer just under the bark) match on at least one side. If the scion and rootstock are different sizes, align one edge perfectly. Wrap tightly with grafting tape or plastic strips, covering the entire cut and the scion's top cut. Seal with wax or a plastic bag to prevent drying. In 2â3 weeks, check for new growth. Remove any shoots from the rootstock below the graft. After 2â3 months, cut the tape carefully. Your new tree will grow true to the scion variety.

lessons.title: The cleft graft: reviving old trees or top-working
lessons.body:
Cleft grafting is the go-to method for changing the variety of an established tree (top-working) or reviving an old tree with a damaged trunk. It works when the rootstock is much larger than the scionâoften 5â15 cm in diameter. In Africa, this is common for improving mango, citrus, and avocado trees that produce poor fruit. Do this in late winter or early spring while the tree is still dormant but sap is beginning to flow.

First, cut off the rootstock branch or trunk squarely with a pruning saw, leaving a clean, flat surface. If the branch is large, you may need to graft on several branches around the tree to balance growth. Use a sharp knife to smooth the cut. Then, with a sturdy grafting chisel or a wide screwdriver, split the stump down the middle to a depth of 5â8 cm. If the wood is hard, tap the chisel with a mallet. The split should be centered.

Prepare scions: Choose dormant wood of the desired variety, 1â2 cm thick and 10â15 cm long with 2â3 buds. Make a long, sloping cut on each side of the base of the scion, about 4â5 cm long, tapering to a point. The cuts should be flat and clean. Insert one scion into each side of the split, with the cambium layers (the green layer under the bark) aligned with the cambium of the rootstock. The scion's sloping cut should face outward. If the rootstock is very large, you can place two scions, one on each side.

Remove the chisel. The split will close and hold the scions tightly. Wrap the entire graft union and the cut surface with grafting tape or plastic strips, and seal all exposed cuts with wax or tree wound paint. Cover the scion tips with wax too. In a few weeks, buds should start growing. Remove any shoots from the rootstock below the graft. After one season, select the strongest shoot and remove the others. This method can turn an old, unproductive tree into a valuable one in 2â3 years.

lessons.title: The side graft: when and how to use it
lessons.body:
The side graft is useful when the rootstock is too large for a whip-and-tongue but you don't want to cut off the entire top (as in cleft grafting). It is ideal for adding a new variety to an existing tree (top-working) without killing the main trunk, or for grafting onto a rootstock that is slightly larger than the scion. In Africa, this technique works well for citrus, mango, and avocado, especially when you want to change only part of a tree or when the rootstock is 2â5 cm in diameter.

Choose a smooth area on the side of the rootstock, about 15â20 cm above the ground or on a main branch. Make a shallow, downward-sloping cut into the bark and wood, about 3â4 cm long, starting at a 30-degree angle. The cut should go just deep enough to expose the cambium (the green layer). Then, on the scion (same diameter as the cut depth, or slightly smaller), make a matching cut: a long, sloping cut on one side, about 3â4 cm long, and a short cut on the opposite side at the base to form a wedge. The scion should have 2â3 buds.

Insert the scion into the cut on the rootstock so the cambium layers match on at least one side. The scion will stick out at an angle. Wrap the union tightly with grafting tape or plastic strips, covering the cut and the scion base. Seal with wax. Do not cut off the rootstock top immediately; leave it to draw sap and keep the tree alive. After 3â4 weeks, check for growth from the scion. If it grows, gradually cut back the rootstock top over several months, a little at a time, to force the scion to take over. Remove any shoots from the rootstock below the graft. This method is slower than cleft grafting but less risky because the tree continues to grow while the graft establishes.

lessons.title: Making clean cuts and matching cambium layers
lessons.body:
The success of any graft depends on two things: clean cuts and matching cambium layers. The cambium is the thin, green layer just under the bark. When you cut, you expose it. For the graft to heal, the cambium of the scion and rootstock must touch and grow together. If they don't, the graft fails.

First, tools: You need a sharp grafting knife. A dull knife crushes cells and makes a rough cut that won't heal. Sharpen your knife before each grafting session. Use a sharpening stone and oil. A good test: the knife should shave hair off your arm. Also, clean your tools with alcohol or bleach solution between trees to prevent disease spread.

Making the cut: For whip-and-tongue, the cuts should be smooth, flat, and long enough to expose plenty of cambium. Make the cut in one continuous motion, not sawing back and forth. For cleft and side grafts, the cuts must be flat and straight. If you make a mistake, cut againâdon't try to patch it. Always cut on a firm surface. Hold the wood securely. Practice on pruned branches before grafting your valuable trees.

Matching cambium: After inserting the scion, look at the union. You want the green layer of the scion to line up with the green layer of the rootstock. If the scion is smaller, align one side perfectly; the other side will have a gap. That's okay as long as one side matches. For cleft grafts, place the scion so the cambium touches the cambium of the rootstock on the outer edge. For side grafts, the same. Use a knife tip to adjust if needed. Once aligned, don't move the pieces. Wrap tightly to hold them in place. Remember: no cambium contact, no graft. With practice, you'll make clean cuts and match layers quickly.

lessons.title: Wrapping and sealing grafts with tape and wax
lessons.body:
After you've inserted the scion and matched the cambium, you must wrap and seal the graft to hold it tight and prevent drying. Without wrapping, the union will dry out and fail. You can use grafting tape, plastic strips, or even cut plastic bags. Wax or tree wound paint seals the exposed cuts.

Wrapping: Start below the graft union and wrap upward, overlapping each turn by half. Pull the tape snugly but not so tight that it cuts into the bark. The tape should cover the entire cut and the scion base. For whip-and-tongue, also wrap the scion's top cut if it's exposed. For cleft and side grafts, wrap the union and the cut surfaces. Use a rubber band or twine if tape is not available, but plastic tape is best because it stretches and seals. In Africa, many farmers use strips of inner tube or plastic bags cut into 1 cm wide strips. Whatever you use, make sure it's clean.

Sealing: After wrapping, seal all exposed cuts with wax or tree wound paint. This includes the top of the scion (if not covered by tape), the cut surfaces on the rootstock, and any gaps. You can buy grafting wax or make your own by melting 1 part beeswax, 1 part rosin, and 1 part paraffin. Apply warm wax with a brush. Alternatively, use melted candle wax. The seal prevents water loss and keeps out disease.

Aftercare: Check the graft every week. If tape loosens, rewrap. If you see new growth from the scion, great. If the scion dries out, it failedâtry again. After 2â3 months, the union should heal. Then carefully cut the tape on one side to avoid girdling the tree. Remove tape completely after 4â6 months. For wax, it will weather away. Always remove any shoots growing from the rootstock below the graft, as they compete with the scion. With proper wrapping and sealing, your graft has a much higher chance of success.

lessons.title: Hands-on: Practicing three grafts on rootstocks
lessons.body:
Now it's time to practice. You'll need rootstocks and scion wood. For practice, use fast-growing local species like citrus (rough lemon or sour orange), mango, or guava. You can also practice on pruned branches of any tree. Get at least 10 rootstocks and 20 scions so you can make mistakes. Work in a shaded area to prevent drying.

Gather your tools: sharp grafting knife, pruning shears, grafting tape, wax, and a sharpening stone. Clean your tools with alcohol. Set up a table. Label your scions with the variety name and date. Practice each graft type at least three times.

First, whip-and-tongue: Choose rootstock and scion of equal thickness (6â10 mm). Make the cuts as described in Lesson 1. Remember to interlock the tongues. Wrap tightly. Do this three times. Second, cleft graft: Use a larger rootstock (2â5 cm diameter). Cut it off, split it, and insert two scions. Wrap and seal. Do this three times. Third, side graft: Use a rootstock 2â5 cm diameter. Make the side cut, insert scion, wrap. Do this three times.

After each graft, check your work: Are the cambium layers matching? Is the wrap tight? Is the wax sealed? If not, redo. Keep a notebook: record the date, graft type, and any problems. After 2â3 weeks, check for growth. Count how many took. With practice, your success rate will improve. In Africa, many farmers learn by doing. Don't be afraid to failâeach failure teaches you. Share your results with neighbors. Grafting is a skill that can increase your fruit production and income.

quiz.q: What is the ideal diameter of rootstock and scion for a whip-and-tongue graft?
quiz.explanation: Whip-and-tongue grafts work best when both scion and rootstock are pencil-thick, about 6â10 mm in diameter.

quiz.q: Which graft method is best for changing the variety of a large, established tree?
quiz.explanation: Cleft grafting is used for top-working large trees because it can handle rootstocks much larger than the scion.

quiz.q: What is the cambium layer?
options: B) The green layer just under the bark
C) The center of the wood
quiz.explanation: The cambium is the thin, green layer under the bark that must be matched for a graft to heal.

quiz.q: When should you collect scion wood for grafting?
options: A) When the tree is actively growing
quiz.explanation: Scion wood should be collected during dormancy to ensure it is firm and has stored energy for the graft.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the 'tongue' in a whip-and-tongue graft?
options: A) To make the graft look nice
B) To interlock the pieces and hold them tight
C) To allow water to drain
quiz.explanation: The tongue interlocks the scion and rootstock, providing mechanical strength while the graft heals.

quiz.q: How deep should you split the rootstock in a cleft graft?
quiz.explanation: The split should be about 5â8 cm deep to accommodate the scion wedges.

quiz.q: What tool is essential for making clean cuts in grafting?
quiz.explanation: A sharp grafting knife makes smooth cuts that heal quickly; dull tools crush cells and cause failure.

quiz.q: In a side graft, what do you do with the rootstock top after the graft takes?
options: C) Gradually cut it back over several months
D) Graft another scion on it
quiz.explanation: The rootstock top is gradually cut back to allow the scion to take over without shocking the tree.

quiz.q: Why is it important to seal grafts with wax?
options: A) To make them look neat
B) To prevent drying and disease
quiz.explanation: Wax seals exposed cuts, preventing water loss and entry of pathogens.

quiz.q: How often should you check grafts after grafting?
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks allow you to fix loose tape, remove rootstock shoots, and monitor for growth.

quiz.q: What is the best time of year to do cleft grafting?
options: B) Late winter or early spring
quiz.explanation: Cleft grafting is done in late winter or early spring while the tree is dormant but sap is beginning to flow.

quiz.q: What should you do if the scion and rootstock are different sizes?
options: B) Align one side's cambium perfectly
C) Cut the larger one down
quiz.explanation: As long as one side's cambium layers match, the graft can succeed.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a reason to clean your grafting tools?
options: C) To keep the knife sharp
D) To make the graft look pretty
quiz.explanation: Cleaning tools prevents disease and ensures sharpness, but aesthetics are not a reason.

quiz.q: What is top-working?
options: A) Grafting onto the top of a tree
B) Changing the variety of an established tree
quiz.explanation: Top-working is the practice of changing the variety of an existing tree by grafting new scions onto its branches.

quiz.q: How long should you wait before removing grafting tape?
quiz.explanation: Tape should be removed after 4â6 months, once the graft has healed, to prevent girdling.

quiz.q: What is a good rootstock for practicing grafting in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Citrus, such as rough lemon, is a common and fast-growing rootstock used in Africa.

quiz.q: What does the cambium do in a graft?
options: B) It forms the new union tissue
quiz.explanation: The cambium cells divide and grow together, forming the permanent union between scion and rootstock.

quiz.q: In a whip-and-tongue graft, how long should the diagonal cuts be?
quiz.explanation: The cuts should be about 3â5 cm long to expose enough cambium for a strong union.

quiz.q: What should you do with shoots growing from the rootstock below the graft?
options: D) Tie them to the scion
quiz.explanation: These shoots compete with the scion for nutrients and should be removed.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of wrapping the graft with tape?
options: A) To hold the pieces tight and prevent drying
B) To make it look neat
quiz.explanation: Tape holds the scion and rootstock firmly together and seals the union to prevent moisture loss.

quiz.q: Which graft is best for a rootstock that is 2â5 cm in diameter but you don't want to cut off the top?
quiz.explanation: Side grafting allows you to add a scion to the side of a larger rootstock without removing its top.

quiz.q: How can you test if your grafting knife is sharp enough?
options: B) It shaves hair off your arm
quiz.explanation: A sharp knife should easily shave hair, indicating it will make clean cuts.

quiz.q: What is the recommended number of buds on a scion for cleft grafting?
quiz.explanation: A scion with 2â3 buds provides enough growing points without being too long.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid sawing back and forth when making a cut?
options: B) It creates a rough surface that won't heal
quiz.explanation: Sawing creates a jagged cut that prevents cambium layers from matching and healing smoothly.

quiz.q: What is a common local material used for wrapping grafts in Africa?
options: B) Plastic bags cut into strips
quiz.explanation: Many farmers use strips of plastic bags or inner tubes as grafting tape.

quiz.q: After a cleft graft, how many scions can you insert if the rootstock is large?
options: B) Two, one on each side
quiz.explanation: For large rootstocks, two scions can be inserted, one on each side of the split, to increase success.

quiz.q: What should you do if the graft fails?
options: B) Try again with new scion and rootstock
quiz.explanation: Grafting requires practice; failures are learning opportunities, so try again.

quiz.q: How long does it typically take for a graft to show new growth?
quiz.explanation: New growth usually appears within 2â3 weeks if the graft was successful.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of the whip-and-tongue graft?
options: A) It works on large trees
B) It gives a strong, natural union
C) It is the easiest to learn
quiz.explanation: The interlocking tongues create a strong union that heals quickly and looks natural.

quiz.q: What should you record in your grafting notebook?
options: A) Date, graft type, and problems
quiz.explanation: Keeping records helps you track success rates and improve your technique over time.
